questions.q: Per this lesson, what is a release strategy?
options: A single deployment's checklist of what's included and who approves it
The organization's standing, in-advance decisions about cadence, environment path, and risk tiers that make every individual deployment plan fast to write
A Salesforce feature that automatically schedules deployments
A document that only applies to Apex code, never to declarative changes
questions.explain: A release strategy is the standing framework of decisions made once, in advance, so that each individual deployment plan doesn't have to re-answer the same hard questions from scratch.

questions.q: How does this lesson distinguish a release strategy from a deployment plan?
options: They are the same thing, just two names for one document
A deployment plan only exists for failed releases
The strategy is the standing framework; the deployment plan is the specific, one-time plan for a single release, built quickly because the strategy already answered the hard questions
A release strategy is written by developers, while a deployment plan is written by executives
questions.explain: The strategy is the reusable framework of decisions; the deployment plan is the one-time application of that framework to a specific release.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say an org's internal release strategy has to account for Salesforce's seasonal release cadence?
options: Because Salesforce ships three mandatory, platform-wide seasonal releases a year on its own schedule, and the org's own cadence has to be built to absorb that external, non-negotiable cycle
Because seasonal releases only affect sandboxes, never production
Because Salesforce lets customers opt out of seasonal releases entirely if they prefer
Because seasonal releases replace the need for any internal change control
questions.explain: Salesforce's three yearly seasonal releases are mandatory and scheduled by Salesforce, not the customer, so an org's own release strategy has to be built around that fixed external cadence rather than ignoring it.

questions.q: A text-field label change and a new Apex trigger on Opportunity are both proposed for the same release. Per this lesson's discussion of risk tolerance and gating, what should a release strategy do about this?
options: Treat them identically, since both are technically "changes"
Block the Apex trigger permanently, since code changes are never allowed
Require the field label change to go through a full regression test suite instead of the trigger
Define risk tiers so the two changes go through different levels of scrutiny appropriate to their actual risk
questions.explain: The lesson states a release strategy should define risk tiers so that a low-risk change like a field label and a higher-risk change like a new trigger don't move through an identical approval process.

questions.q: Per this lesson, when should a release strategy be revisited?
options: Never — once written, it should stay fixed permanently
Only when Salesforce forces a change through a seasonal release
When the organization's risk profile changes, when team size or structure changes, or when a retrospective reveals a gap the current strategy doesn't cover
Only once per decade, regardless of what changes in the organization
questions.explain: The lesson describes a release strategy as a living document that gets revisited as risk profile, team structure, or retrospective findings change — not a one-time, permanently fixed artifact.
